title: Pressure & Density - Application
welcome_lead: Dive into pressure underwater and what makes things float.
meta_desc: KS3 Physics: applying density and pressure to floating and fluids.
final_note: Outstanding! You can now predict what sinks and floats.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Liquids and gases push in all directions because their particles bump everything around them.

The deeper you go, the more fluid above you, the higher the pressure.

Submarines must be strong enough to handle huge pressure at depth - or they get crushed!

Right now, the atmosphere pushes on you with about 100,000 pascals of pressure.

You don't feel it because it pushes from all sides equally.

Up a mountain, less air sits above you, so pressure is lower - that's why ears pop when you climb or fly.

If an object is less dense than the fluid, it floats.

If it's more dense, it sinks.

Wood floats on water because wood density (~0.6 g/cm³) is less than water (1 g/cm³).

A metal ship floats because its overall density (including air inside) is less than water - even though metal alone would sink!

Your eyes send out beams of vision that hit the book and let you see it.

Light from a source reflects off the book and enters your eyes.

options: The voltage across the wire creates magnetism.
Yes — UV is the colour purple.
No — even though it sits next to violet on the spectrum, its frequency is above the range our eyes detect.
Yes — UV is visible because it's right next to violet.
